blocks.html:
Should we stop eating meat?

Some claim that it's the only way to save our planet from disaster. But is it really that simple?

A The call for people to eat less meat to save the planet is growing louder, so if less is good, wouldn't none be better? To find out, let's imagine what would happen if the world eliminated meat, milk and eggs from its diet, then trace the effects. Last year the world consumed 289 million tonnes of meat, 700 million tonnes of milk and 1.2 billion eggs. Environmentally speaking, this came at an enormous cost.

B All agriculture damages the environment. Take for example the felled forests and the common use of irrigation systems. And it may surprise you to know that agriculture creates more greenhouse gases than all methods of transport put together. Livestock farming does the most damage. In part, that is because most livestock eat grain that could be used to feed human populations, and farmers are forced to grow more than we would otherwise need to meet the demand. Altogether, if we switched to a vegan diet, meaning no meat, dairy or eggs, the land currently required for crops would drop by an estimated 21 per cent, about 3.4 million hectares, roughly the size of India.

C One environmental impact that would also lessen through a reduction in animal farming would be that of the nitrogen emitted from agricultural processes, which spreads into both waterways and land. According to environmental scientist Allison Leach, if everyone eliminated dairy products and eggs, this kind of pollution would fall by 60%. Livestock production has another serious environmental impact. Global statistics are hard to come by, but in the US at least, livestock account for 55% of erosion, mostly from forests being cut down to make way for grazing land. On top of this, half of all antibiotics manufactured are fed to livestock as part of their normal diet, a practice that is leading to drug-resistant bacteria.

D A meat-free world, then would be greener in many ways. However, if everyone opted to give up meat there would be significant costs too. For most of human history, livestock grazed on land that wasn't suitable for ploughing, and in doing so they converted inedible grass into edible meat and milk. Even today, a flock of sheep or goats can be the most efficient way to get food from marginal land. In a world in which over a billion people do not have enough to eat, using this land for crop production would contribute to food insecurity.

E In some parts of the world today, livestock like chickens, for instance, can subsist on leftovers and whatever they find. Tara Garnett, who heads the Food Climate Research Network at the University of Surrey, points out the usefulness of these animals. By giving them your leftovers, she says, they deal with your rubbish, and you get meat. Garnett admits, though, that if this kind of approach were generally adopted, it would require a major adjustment in food preferences; people would have to get used to chicken, for example, with less fat.

F Another downside to a meat-free world would be the disappearance of animal by-products. Such a world would have to replace the 11 million tonnes of leather and 2 million tonnes of wool that come annually from livestock farming and which are turned into clothing. Furthermore, even ardent vegetarians acknowledge that dairy products and meat may be a good thing in poorer countries. ‘Whilst there's no doubt that considerable reduction of meat consumption would have an environmental benefit, we do have to be careful about saying it would be the best solution if the whole world went vegetarian,' says Annette Pinner, chief executive of the UK Vegetarian Society. For many of the world's poorest rural residents, an animal may represent their only realistic hope for a little extra income, and a little animal protein can make a big difference to a marginal diet.

G What if we decided on a no-meat vegetarian diet, rather than a vegan diet? After all, milk and eggs are very efficient ways of producing animal calories. ‘It's difficult to switch to a no-meat-but-milk diet,' says Helmut Haberl, a social ecologist. 'Dairy cows must calve every year to keep producing milk, and only half their offspring will be female. While many vegetarians see moral reasons not to kill and eat the males, there is surely no practical reason to waste so much meat.' Similar arguments apply to chickens kept for eggs.

H So even though a meat-free world sounds good on paper, it is likely that a utopian future will still have some animal products in it. The real questions, then, are how much meat do we want, and how will we produce it? The answers depend on how you approach these questions. The most straightforward approach is to assume that the world will continue to want evermore meat. The United Nations' best guess is that by 2050, the world will need to more than double its production of meat, an increase that would be environmentally disastrous.

I Under this scenario the goal will have to be producing the most meat at the lowest environmental cost. According to Walter Falcon, an agricultural economist, this means fewer free range cattle and sheep in green fields. 'If you're going to keep some livestock systems, I think the ones you'll want to keep are the intensive ones,' he says. Of course this does not take into account animal welfare issues, as intensive farming usually means poor living conditions and the use of growth hormones.

Questions 18–22

Complete the summary below.

Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.

How does agriculture damage the environment?

Agriculture causes significant harm to the environment in a number of ways, including the frequent use of 18 in modern farming and the cutting down of trees. It is also responsible for the production of many greenhouse gases, more so than 19 is. However, it is livestock farming in particular that is most harmful, because cows, chickens and sheep, for example, are given vast quantities of grain which could be consumed by people instead. A meat-free diet would mean that actually less 20 could be used for crops. Far less chemical pollution, specifically in the form of 21 , would also be released into the environment, especially if consumers cut out dairy and egg products as well as meat. In the US, there is clear evidence that considerable 22 is caused by the demand for grazing land, although there is no information on this from other countries.

Questions 23–26

Look at the following statements (Questions 23–26) and the list of people below.

Match each statement with the correct researcher, A–E.

passageNotes.label: Paragraph A
passageNotes.text: 呼吁人们少吃肉以拯救地球的声音越来越响亮，那么如果少吃是好事，完全不吃岂不是更好？为了弄清这一点，让我们想象一下如果全世界从饮食中去除肉类、牛奶和鸡蛋会发生什么，然后追溯其影响。去年，全世界消费了2.89亿吨肉类、7亿吨牛奶和12亿枚鸡蛋。从环境角度来看，这一切付出了巨大的代价。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph B
passageNotes.text: 所有农业都会对环境造成损害。以砍伐森林和灌溉系统的普遍使用为例。而且你可能会惊讶地发现，农业产生的温室气体比所有交通方式加起来还多。畜牧业造成的破坏最大。部分原因是，大多数牲畜吃的谷物本可以用来养活人类人口，而农民被迫种植比我们原本需要的更多的粮食来满足需求。总的来说，如果我们转向纯素饮食（即不吃肉类、乳制品或鸡蛋），目前用于农作物的土地预计将减少21%，约340万公顷，大致相当于印度的面积。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph C
passageNotes.text: 减少畜牧业还会减轻的另一个环境影响是农业过程中排放的氮，这些氮会扩散到水道和土地中。根据环境科学家Allison Leach的说法，如果每个人都停止食用乳制品和鸡蛋，这类污染将减少60%。畜牧业还有另一个严重的环境影响。全球统计数据很难获得，但至少在美国，畜牧业占水土流失的55%，主要是由于砍伐森林以开辟牧场。除此之外，制造的所有抗生素中有一半被作为日常饲料的一部分喂给牲畜，这种做法正在导致耐药细菌的产生。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph D
passageNotes.text: 因此，一个无肉的世界在许多方面会更加绿色。然而，如果每个人都选择放弃肉类，也会带来巨大的代价。在人类历史的大部分时间里，牲畜在不适合耕种的土地上吃草，通过这种方式，它们将不可食用的草转化为可食用的肉类和牛奶。即使在今天，一群绵羊或山羊可能是从贫瘠土地上获取食物的最有效方式。在一个有超过十亿人食不果腹的世界里，将这些土地用于农作物生产将加剧粮食不安全问题。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph E
passageNotes.text: 在当今世界的某些地区，像鸡这样的牲畜可以靠残羹剩饭和它们能找到的任何东西存活。萨里大学食品气候研究网络负责人Tara Garnett指出了这些动物的用处。她说，把剩饭剩菜给它们，它们帮你处理垃圾，你还能得到肉类。不过Garnett承认，如果这种做法被普遍采用，将需要对食物偏好进行重大调整；例如，人们将不得不习惯脂肪含量更低的鸡肉。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph F
passageNotes.text: 无肉世界的另一个不利之处是动物副产品的消失。这样一个世界将不得不取代畜牧业每年产出的1100万吨皮革和200万吨羊毛，这些材料被制成服装。此外，即使是坚定的素食主义者也承认，在较贫穷的国家，乳制品和肉类可能是好事。英国素食协会首席执行官Annette Pinner表示：“虽然毫无疑问，大幅减少肉类消费会对环境有益，但我们必须谨慎对待这样的说法——如果全世界都成为素食者，那就是最佳解决方案。”对于世界上最贫穷的农村居民来说，一头牲畜可能代表着他们唯一现实的增加少量收入的希望，而少量的动物蛋白质可以对勉强维持温饱的饮食产生重大影响。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph G
passageNotes.text: 如果我们决定采用无肉的素食饮食，而不是纯素饮食，会怎样呢？毕竟，牛奶和鸡蛋是生产动物热量的非常高效的方式。社会生态学家Helmut Haberl说：“转向无肉但有奶的饮食是困难的。奶牛必须每年产犊才能继续产奶，而它们的后代只有一半是母牛。虽然许多素食主义者认为有道德上的理由不宰杀和食用公牛，但浪费这么多肉肯定没有任何实际理由。”类似的论点也适用于为产蛋而饲养的鸡。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph H
passageNotes.text: 因此，尽管无肉的世界听起来在纸面上很美好，但一个乌托邦式的未来很可能仍然会包含一些动物产品。那么，真正的问题是，我们想要多少肉，以及我们将如何生产它？答案取决于你如何处理这些问题。最直接的方法是假设世界将继续需要越来越多的肉类。联合国的最佳预测是，到2050年，世界将需要将其肉类产量增加一倍以上，而这种增长在环境方面将是灾难性的。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph I
passageNotes.text: 在这种情况下，目标必须是以最低的环境成本生产最多的肉类。农业经济学家Walter Falcon表示，这意味着绿色田野上自由放牧的牛羊将会减少。他说：“如果你要保留一些畜牧业体系，我认为你想保留的是集约化的那一种。”当然，这并没有考虑到动物福利问题，因为集约化养殖通常意味着恶劣的生活条件和使用生长激素。
